question: How do honeybees tell other bees where to find flowers?
answer: They perform a waggle dance inside the hive that encodes the direction and distance of the flowers.

retriever_a: A honeybee colony in summer can hold forty thousand workers, a single queen and a few hundred drones. Workers change jobs as they age: young bees clean cells and feed larvae, middle-aged bees build comb and guard the entrance, and the oldest bees fly out to gather nectar and pollen.

Inside the dark hive, a returning forager runs in a short straight line while shaking her body, then loops back and repeats. Other workers follow her closely. The angle of that straight run, measured from vertical on the comb, matches the angle between the sun and the food, and the length of the run tells the distance to the flowers.

Nectar is carried back to the hive in a special stomach and passed from bee to bee. As the bees fan the thin liquid with their wings, water evaporates until the sugary syrup thickens into honey, which is sealed under a thin cap of wax for the winter months.

Flowers that rely on bees are often blue, purple or yellow and frequently carry ultraviolet patterns that are invisible to people. These patterns act like landing strips that guide a visiting bee toward the nectar at the centre of the bloom.

Beekeepers have long noticed that when one forager finds a rich patch of clover, dozens of hive mates soon arrive at the same patch. The forager advertises the find by dancing on the comb; the excited pattern of the dance tells the other workers that the food is worth collecting and roughly where it is.

On cold mornings honeybees cluster tightly around the queen and shiver their flight muscles to produce heat. The cluster slowly rotates so that bees on the chilly outer layer move inward to warm up while others take their place.

Bees keep track of the sun's position even when it is hidden by cloud, because their eyes detect the polarisation pattern of the sky. This helps a forager fly a straight line home after wandering across a meadow for an hour.

question: Why are there two high tides each day on most coasts?
answer: The moon's gravity raises a bulge of water on the side of the earth facing it and another on the far side, and the earth rotates through both bulges each day.

These are called spring tides, though they have nothing to do with the season. When the sun and moon pull at right angles, the tides are smaller and are called neap tides.

Harbour masters publish tide tables months in advance. The tables list the time and height of each high and low water, and fishermen use them to decide when a boat can safely cross a sandbar at the mouth of the river.

The moon pulls the ocean toward itself, raising a bulge of water on the side of the earth that faces it. A second bulge forms on the far side, where the water is pulled less strongly than the solid earth beneath it. As the planet turns once a day, every coast passes through both bulges, which is why most shores see two high tides.

The shape of a coastline changes how big the tides are. In a long, narrowing bay the incoming water is squeezed and can rise by more than ten metres, while on a small island in the open ocean the difference between high and low water may be less than a metre.

question: Why does bread dough rise while it rests?
answer: Yeast feeds on sugars in the flour and releases carbon dioxide, which is trapped by the gluten network and inflates the dough.

retriever_a: A sourdough starter is a jar of flour and water in which wild yeasts and bacteria have settled. It must be fed fresh flour every day or two, and the bacteria produce the acids that give sourdough its sharp flavour and long shelf life.

Bread yeast is a living fungus. When it is mixed into flour and water it begins to feed on the sugars that the flour releases, and as it feeds it gives off carbon dioxide and a little alcohol. The gas is what makes the dough swell; the alcohol mostly bakes away in the oven.

The crust turns brown in the oven because sugars and proteins on the surface react in the heat. Bakers spray water into the oven during the first minutes of baking so that the surface stays soft a little longer and the loaf can expand fully before the crust sets.

Wheat flour contains two proteins that, when wet and kneaded, join into a stretchy web called gluten. This web is elastic enough to hold the bubbles of gas produced during rising, so instead of escaping, the gas inflates the dough like thousands of tiny balloons.

Kneading is the folding and pushing that turns a shaggy mass into a smooth ball. Ten minutes of kneading by hand is usually enough; the dough is ready when a small piece can be stretched thin enough to see light through without tearing.

Bakers put dough in a warm corner of the kitchen for a reason. Yeast works faster as the temperature rises toward body heat, so warm dough doubles in size in an hour, while dough left in a cold pantry may take most of a day to rise.

Salt does more than season bread. It slows the yeast slightly so the dough rises evenly, tightens the dough so it holds its shape, and helps the crust colour. Bread made without salt tastes flat and rises so fast that it often collapses.

The rising of dough is simply yeast breathing. It consumes the sugars in the flour and exhales carbon dioxide, and it breathes faster when warm. This is why a bowl of dough set near a warm stove rises in a fraction of the time it takes in a cool room.

question: When was the covered bridge at Marlow Bend built, and why does it have a roof?
answer: It was built in 1852, and it was roofed to protect its wooden trusses from rain and snow.

The Marlow River is shallow and fast for most of its length, tumbling over gravel bars that make it popular with people who fish for trout. Only at the bend does it slow and deepen, which is why the village grew up on that spot.

The covered bridge at Marlow Bend was completed in 1852 by a crew of local carpenters led by a millwright named Abel Corrigan. It replaced a ferry that had carried farm carts across the river since the village was founded, and it is the oldest structure in the county still in daily use.

A grist mill stood just downstream of the village until a flood carried it away. Its millstones were dug out of the riverbank years later and now sit at the entrance to the town library, where children like to climb on them.

People sometimes assume the roof of a covered bridge was meant to shelter travellers, but its real purpose was to protect the timber. An uncovered wooden truss soaked by rain and snow would rot within a decade or two, while a roofed and sided bridge could last a century.

question: Why does a rainbow have the shape of an arc?
answer: Sunlight leaves each raindrop at a fixed angle of about 42 degrees, so the drops that send colour to your eye lie on a circle around the point opposite the sun, and the ground hides the lower part of that circle.

Sunlight enters a raindrop, bends, reflects off the back of the drop and bends again on the way out. For red light the total turn is about 42 degrees from the direction of the incoming sunlight. Every drop that sits at that angle from the line between the sun and your eye sends red light to you, and those drops form a circle around the point opposite the sun.

A second, fainter rainbow sometimes appears outside the first with its colours reversed. It is produced by light that reflects twice inside each drop. Between the two bows the sky looks noticeably darker, a region that has been given the name of a medieval scholar.

From an aeroplane or a high mountain a rainbow can be seen as a complete circle, because there are raindrops below the observer as well as above. On the ground the lower part of the circle would be beneath the horizon, so only the upper arc is visible.

Because the bow is defined by the angle between the sun, the drops and the observer's eye, two people standing side by side see rainbows made by different drops. It is impossible to walk to the end of a rainbow: as you move, the bow moves with you.

question: How can sailors tell which lighthouse they are looking at during the night?
answer: Each lighthouse flashes in its own timed pattern, called its characteristic, and nautical charts list these patterns so sailors can match the flashes to a named light.

No two lighthouses within sight of each other flash the same way. One may give a single flash every five seconds, another two quick flashes every ten, and a third a steady light with a brief eclipse. This timed pattern is called the light's characteristic, and it is the lighthouse's signature.

When fog hides the light, a lighthouse sounds a horn instead. Like the flashes, the blasts follow a timed pattern, but sound bends and echoes in ways that light does not, so sailors treat the horn as a warning rather than a precise fix.

On a nautical chart each lighthouse is marked with a short code such as Fl(2) 10s, meaning two flashes every ten seconds. A navigator who sees a light on the horizon times the flashes with a watch, finds the matching code on the chart, and knows which headland lies ahead.

In daylight a lighthouse is identified by its daymark: the colour and pattern of its tower. Red and white bands, black and white spirals or a plain white column make each tower recognisable from a distance without any light at all.
